The columbus ohio play group has had a brief discussion about the
balance of the card game we're here to discuss... In general, there
was some off topic remarks and then some digression about specific
cards being more powerful than others, and some disciplines being
better than others, and that some vampires were costed better than
others.

I would like to hear this forum's thoughts on this issue. With in your
post, please remark if you find VTES to be balanced or not, and give
some reasons why you think it has balance, and I would also like you
to comment on a statement I've typed below.

Here is my stance.

VTES is a card game based off of a RPG. Balance is not neccesarily an
issue in RPGs, as there are storytellers that can tweak balances. CCGs
have similar balance controllers known as game designers. Storytellers
can scrap certain story lines, or characters, if their effect on the
game world is too severe. Game designers (specifically white wolf) can
not do so. This is my first point.

With in this RPG there are clans of vampires that use 3 different
disciplines more than other disciplines. The same has been done for
the CCG. Each discipline has certain things it can do. Some vampires
were released for this game, after developing a majority of the cards
they can use (discipline related cards). Who decides if these
vampires, with X Y and Z disciplines are balanced? The game designer.
What desides what skills certain vampires will have? The RPG. Hence,
there is a lack of balance.

VTES may SEEM balanced, as the factors that make VTES unbalanced are
set off by the fact that it is a multiplayer game, which creates its
own sort of (im)balances. Hence, VTES is NOT balanced, but only
appears to be so, due to the multiplayer aspect of the game.
Furthermore, being a VTES game designer would be a posh hack job as
you could print nearly anything as long as it fit the RPG feel and
wasn't a "you win" card.

Flame on.
~SV

Ideally, the CCG finds a way to make every discipline or at least the primary

amount of room for adapting thematics, so it's possible.

>appears to be so, due to the multiplayer aspect of the game.

With respect to balancing who wins and loses, it helps tremendously for a CCG
to be multiplayer - everyone gangs up on the leader(s) to the ability they are
able. The best thing about V:TES, possibly ironically, is that it limits the
incentives and ability to take down the leader which results in *gasp* good
play and good deck design sort of mattering (though, a relatively high number
of recent discussions about the game have been about how little deck design has
mattered and how much good play comes down to convincing people you aren't as
strong as you are).

My problem with the game balance is that, on the individual action level, the
game is highly unbalanced. Bleed for 6? Send your main vamp to torpor? Bad
stuff. But, because of the multiplayer dynamic and maybe something else, the
high level game balance is far superior to the individual action balance.

In terms of aspects of the game, I believe that there's numerous imbalances
between disciplines, discipline combinations, vampires, and clans. This is
solvable to some degree. Clans that can't put together good discipline combos
as easily can get better clan cards or better vampires. And, so forth. While
I've seen elevation of weaker clans (see Final Nights) to respectable levels, I
believe there's more room for trying to balance clans and other aspects. It
looks like one of my concerns - improving weaker disciplines (via 3-ways) -
could be addressed with Anarchs. Yet, for instance, while a number of weaker
clans have gotten better, I haven't seen much effort put into bringing the
elite clans down a peg either by making other clans as good or better or by
doing something that actually weakens a top clan significantly (the former
being a better way to go). If what I'm talking about isn't clear, there's
never, ever been a time when Malks weren't one of the best clans in the game;
this makes the game staler than it needs to be.

>Furthermore, being a VTES game designer would be a posh hack job as
>you could print nearly anything as long as it fit the RPG feel and
>wasn't a "you win" card.

Um, no. Make a game less fun, and it eventually will bite you on the ass. So,
there's a strong incentive to minimize mistakes.

Depends on your definition of balanced.

All players have an equal chance of winning? No.
All decks have an equal chance of winning? No.
All players with comparably powered decks have an equal chance of
winning? No.
All players with comparable card collections have an equal chance of
winning? No.
All clans have an equal chance of winning? No.
All discipline mixes have an equal chance of winning? No.
All comparably powered decks have an equal chance of winning? No.

All comparably powered decks played by comparably powered players have
an equal chance of winning? Yes.

Real world likelihood of that happening: nil.

No?

No. Why? Because we can only see the game in it's current state. If the

vermillian wrote:

> Who decides if these
> vampires, with X Y and Z disciplines are balanced? The game designer.
> What desides what skills certain vampires will have? The RPG. Hence,
> there is a lack of balance.

There is a lack of balance in terms of the general utility amongst the clan
discipline sets, yes. Certain clans have discipline sets that work really
well together in the CCG, in terms of actually winning games (like the
Malkavians, Ventrue, and Brujah) where others don't (like the Nosferatu,
Gangrel, and Tremere). This being said, there is nothing saying that you
have to use all three disciplines, and two or one discipline strategies work
just fine, and as such, this tends to minimize the disparity between the
clans. For instance, yeah, the Ventrue can use all three disciplines they
have together effectively and make game winning decks, where the Gangrel
can't so much. On the other hand, the Gangrel can do just fine using nothing
but Protean, and gain advantage from only having to focus on one discipline
(in terms of average vampire size and card flow).

So yeah, if people were *required* to use a solitary clan and were
*required* to use all three disciplines in a given deck, your argument would
be sound. As this isn't the case, the game tends to self balance.

>
> VTES may SEEM balanced, as the factors that make VTES unbalanced are
> set off by the fact that it is a multiplayer game, which creates its
> own sort of (im)balances. Hence, VTES is NOT balanced, but only
> appears to be so, due to the multiplayer aspect of the game.

The multi-player aspect of the game has much less of an effect on the game
environment than most folks seem to believe. When the game works, people
focus on their prey, and the multi-player dynamic becomes minimized. When
people ignore this (like by randomly attacking folks across the table or
refusing to oust their prey), they generally don't win, so this is also self
balancing.

> Furthermore, being a VTES game designer would be a posh hack job as
> you could print nearly anything as long as it fit the RPG feel and
> wasn't a "you win" card.

But see, they don't do that. They make balanced cards (generally speaking)
that work well in relation to what already exists.

apply to his prey in order to win, or how much pressure to apply to
his predator to help his deck get going. If the deck suites the
player's style, or any of the player's styles as the case may be, then
the player isn't forced to try to play anything foreign to his system.

Overall, i find VTES to be a balanced game. i think there are three or
perhaps four levels at which balance is built into the game.

[1] The predator-prey dynamic balances the game because you have to
oust your prey[s] to win, whilst balancing this with defence against
your predator. All this involves balancing your use of resources.
[2] The multi-player nature of the game means that you have to pay
attention to the actions of the rest of the table, aiming for balance
which is ideally only upset in YOUR favour.
[3] Whilst some cards and clans are stronger than others, none is
grossly over/underpowered: and even relatively weak clans and cards
almost all have a use as the rock against which a particular set of
scissors will inexorably smash [eg Tremere are designed to do in
Ventrue, eg clan hosers].
[4] The unique nature of most vampires combined with the contesting
rule means that even if someone DID come up with a hideous
game-breaking deck it would fall to contesting, so there is an
ultimate balancing mechanism for almost any conceivable abuse. Related
to this [actually, because of it] there is a phenomenon in VTES
similar to balancing/frequency-dependent selection in genetics, ie it
pays to be different. As in genetics, this creates balance.

>What about Mr. Newbie who rushes cross table "cause it'd be fun"?

(Assuming a grand-prey rush)

"Hey, look guys, he's cross-rushing me for fun. That gives my predator
an easy ride. So, Mr Grand Predator, you really want your prey to be
able to walk all over me? Mr Predator, I'm not going to be able to put
any pressure on my Prey, so when you get to him, his defences will all
be super-tight. And Mr Grand Prey, look, you're not getting any Victory
Points this way."

Jyhad is inherently *designed* as a game that involves an element of
diplomacy. You get to make deals. If someone is being an idiot, show
other players why it's in their interests to stop him.

This is similarly a facet of any multi-player game, however. Anyone
can make a stupid decision, to spite you, if they want. This does not
mean that all multi-player games are inherently unbalanced, however.

>Ye, but some cards were initially designed to be used primarily by X
>clan and later Y clan comes out that can use half of X clans cards,
>and combine those with the awesome sweet cards from Z clan. (where X,
>Z are clans initially released by WotC and Y clan is something new,
>based on WW literature, that WW has released for the CCG).

This works on the assumption that later cards haven't been designed
knowing this.

Putting in super-hosing restrictions on a vampire is not the only option
to follow.

One option includes giving a clan a really screwy set of vampires.
Sure, they might get DIS DIS DIS (insert the three disciplines you feel
would be strongest) but they only get 8 and 9 caps. Or the out of clan
disciplines they get are particularly screwy.

One further option involves paying attention to what disciplines you
give them at which levels. You don't have to give them all OBF DOM PRE.
Careful use of inferiors and out of clan disciplines allows for great
subtlety. So, DIS1 DIS2 DIS3 on a 6 cap, like a Cookie Cutter Sabbat
vampire. Maybe. But how about DIS1 dis2 dis3 pro and a special
instead? That still works out to 6 points of ability, roughly, but you
get a very different vampire, functionally. Then you get the subtlety
of working out which disciplines are 'stronger'. A vampire with: 6 cap
DOM for pre pro Primogen, for example, would play differently to FOR dom
pre pro Primogen. Similarly, they'd play very differently to DOM FOR
PRE.

Then, there is nothing saying that you *HAVE* to introduce the
Harbingers of Skulls. You can be guided by the RPG canon without being
ruled by it. If a combination looks particularly abusive, you can side-
step it. There are a great number of things that could be implemented.

Further, canon is hugely diverse. Any named vampire, for a start, often
has several disciplines in the RPG which they don't have in the CCG.
(The oft-debated 'How would you implement....?' questions.) So you get
a wide range of possibilities in terms of implementation. They also
progress through story-lines, so you get to implement them at a point
you feel comfortable with. Perhaps earlier on, they're more of a
neonate. So implement them then. Or later on, they've been cursed.
Implement them then.

Then vampires within canon are numerous. Implement the vampires you
want. So, Moncada might be difficult to implement, if we were looking
at the Sabbat. You could implement someone else instead. Or you can
make up your own. There's nothing that means that *EVERY* vampire has
to come from canon. So you get considerable latitude to mess with a
clan. Introduce a curve-ball, who's too kooky for the straight-forward
aspect. For instance, Lisette Vizquel is a fantastic vampire from my
point of view - but she's odd for the Lasombra, so you can do
interesting things by scuppering individual vampires. Provide vampires
who are useful for cross-discipline decks, whilst being slightly less
key for clan-based decks.

Then there's the option of rebalancing other aspects of the game. If
there is a discipline combination that means you Just Win, it might be
worth looking at it and examining why. Provide extra options to other
strategies. Indeed, it would be hard for any given 3 discipline
combination to cover *all* bases. If you're sat next to a rush deck, do
you have combat defence? If you're sat next to a vote deck, do you have
vote defence? If you're sat next to a bleed deck, do you have bleed
defence? Can you get your own actions through? Will that need stealth?
Vote pushing? What else? The Ventrue, for instance, get good combat
defence, but can't hit back easily. Once they run out of combat
defence, the vampires can come back again and hit them. They get good
bleed options, and good bleed defence options (bounce). But they get
relatively poor options at getting their actions through. Those
vampires who do get Obfuscate are either expensive or lack titles.
Catherine DuBois is a nice weenie, but lacks the title. The next
cheapest vampire is Suhailah - an excellent example of the above forces
at work. She is a Prince with Obfuscate and Fortitude, but lacks
Dominate or Presence, making her a clever but difficult option.

Which discipline options are going to suddenly cover all the bases
anyway? Most of the Bloodlines disciplines are hampered by their
relative scarcity. They have some very nice powers, but are buggered by
only being found on four or five vampires.

If your have a clan that requires one of those disciplines that's going
to cause a huge problem in the game, you can always not implement them.

Which discipline combination, though, is going to suddenly overpower a
clan that careful design considerations can't mitigate against?
Something with DOM, probably. Well, we all know that the non-neo
Malkavians and the Lasombra are often regarded (and with good reason) as
being the best offensive bleeders with regards such. But they have
problems. They can't get all their bleeds through how they want -
they're still vulnerable to bleed bounce, or rush. Well, there's not so
much we can do about bleed bounce. So how about combat? Well, we might
then say, hmm, combat defence. Fortitude is a good option, as is
Presence. Combining it with some pro-combat might be an option. Maybe
Potence. DOM POT PRE. Nice combination. Or DOM ANI FOR, providing
some bleed, some intercept, some random combat goodness and some combat
defence.

DOM PRO <something> might perturb people. Again, you can simply not
implement that. There's plenty of stuff to do. Or you can provide the
clan with large, costly vampires and few ways to recoup pool. Deny them
titles and any political power, making them vulnerable to any vote
decks. Add a clan disadvantage - Scarce-ity, Sterility, that sort of
thing. Only make a few vampires. Screw up the discipline spread on the
vampires.

Then there's the very simple fact that LSJ has repeatedly stated that
the costing 'formula' is not a simple pick and choose menu. If the
vampires are good, make people pay for them. Just because you've given
them DOM OBF PRO (which for the sake of argument, we'll regard as the
uber discipline spread - though it lacks coherent intercept, or much
pro-combat that can't be foiled with a minimum of combat defence or
isn't rather expensive) doesn't mean that the dom/obf/pro vampire has to
be a 4 cap. Hmm... that's our nastiest combination. *Make it more
expensive*. A 5 cap dom/obf/pro is not entirely unfeasible. If the
discipline spread is worth it, you'll still get a viable clan. (If it

then you built a poor deck. Well, not necessarily poor per se, but you
built in your own problems. By having a 7 capacity vampire who, if
contested, will ruin your game, you've built a deck with no redundancy.

you might not. Bear in mind that if losing your 7 cap vampire ruins
your game, it could just as easily be a pre-emptive rush. Your weenie
combat predator rushes you and destroys it. Just as ruined. Your prey
Banishes it (an early well-timed use of Zillah's Valley, perhaps, and
you were last on the table to go, so when you bring out your 7 cap, he's
also had two goes, and 9 pool has moved - 1 Zillah's Valley, 1
influence, 4 influence. Or 2 extra transfers from Info Highway, twice.
That sort of thing.) Or someone Pentex Subverts you. Or... there are
many ways of hurting a single vampire.

to be re-thought. Or should accept that it was a potentially poor
choice to start with, and that was the chance it took.

>> vote-pushing, repeat actions, Temptation of Greater Power.

>the best bleed and best bleed defense in the game.

Sure you can. Write new cards. Give some other discipline some
fantastic bleed defence. Or some usable bleed defence, if not the best,
and it's still got other abilities anyway so it'll work out differently
anyway. I get some usable bleed defence, and a great array of vote
intimidation, for instance. Or some offensive bleed, along with some
screw-ball antics too.

Or make it less of an issue. Sure, there might be great bleed defence
but Enticement will screw with it. Choir will screw with it.
Individual actions which facilitate different deck designs allow for
great inroads to be made. This is very much the point of politics.
It's there and it side-steps any bleed defence (other than the strategy
of Intercept as Bleed Defence, which is perfectly valid, but also hard)
by virtue of going a different way.

Hosers are also possible. So, Dominate is the best Discipline for bleed
defence, right? Hmm... so I'll write a card that makes my bleed harder
to defend against with Dominate. I'll call it Perfect Clarity. Or I'll
screw up Dominate's bleed offence with a card I'll call Blessing of
Chaos.

>Its these
>abilities, or mechanics if you will that they can't change.

Can't? Clearly not true. Carefully targeted errata and carefully
targeted bans have CLEARLY altered the 'mechanics' of the game. (I
would tend to use 'mechanics' to refer to the facilities established by
rules interaction, rather than what cards and abilities a discipline has
access to already.) Dominate had one of the best combat cards in the
game - Thoughts Betrayed. It now has a fairly interesting combat card,
but not a show-stopper. It still sees use - Xian is a testament to
this, even if no-one else uses it ;-p - but it doesn't completely
outrank all other combat defence in the game. So that
ability/'mechanic' has been altered.

Careful rules re-writes have also prevented certain abusive deck-styles.
For instance, No Repeat Actions has limited a number of deck styles - a
similar rule is part of the base set. Various re-writes of the Vote
Pushing rule have been incorporated into the rules. These mechanics
have been altered also.

Grouping also provides for some really careful and subtle changes.
Group [1/2] excels at various things. What will [2/3] excel at? You
can make them the perfect foils of [1/2] with some careful thought. The
obvious example goes back to the Ventrue - group 1 has great titles,
little stealth. Group 2 and 3 have good stealth, but more expensive
titles. And the problem 'mechanic' of Fifth Tradition/Minion Tap as a
way of neutering the increased cost has been addressed, without
neutering it.

>> To reiterate, i find that VTES IS a balanced game. Absolutely
>> balanced? No. Desirable that it should be? Also no. YMMV.
>
>I just want more games that are closer. I see too many games where one
>guy dominates the table. See other responses to posts I've given.

Perhaps you should play better?

If one person is dominating the table, turning up with a better deck, a
more flexible deck, a longer lasting deck, a more defensive deck, a
faster deck, a more offensive deck, a stronger deck, a harder deck -
whatever you want - is always possible. If you want a better chance at
winning a game, play better.

If a player has the best deck on a given table and plays best, he
*should* win. (Barring randomness really causing grief, which can
happen, even with large amounts of mitigation - all your votes shuffle
to the top, none of you vote push does, and all your cycling cards are
in the bottom 20 cards of the deck.) If the game is so much closer that
the outcome is still very much in flux, despite him having the best deck
and the best play on the table, what's desirable about that? You might
as well roll dice.

If you can tell at half a dozen turns in who definitely is going to win,
look to your own deck. If you're playing competitive snakes and ladders
(that is, any game where it is essentially one player doing things, with
little interaction), expand your deck. If you can't outplay him, why
not? Why did you not build a deck that's capable of letting you win?
Why did you not put in the cards that let you control the table, not
him?

If a game doesn't allow a player to win when he plays better than you,
why should he play?

If you want a game where you can win, despite having a deck that isn't
as good as his and not playing as well, why should anyone play?

Messages.Author: Eric Simon
Messages.Body:
I'm going to agree with lots of the points made her, particularly by
legbiter and lehrbuch. I especially like legbiter's comparison to
genetics, because I think that's a very important analogy to remember.
I'll make my brief comment, which is somewhat a summary and somewhat
a clarification of what many have already said, and then explain it:

You cannot win a V:TES game without the cooperation of other people.

Let me back up to how I came up with that statement. Let's think of
the "ideal" table - everyone has a reasonably balanced deck and is
pursuing their prey in one way or another while attempting to defend
somewhat against their predator. No deals are made, no votes are
called that benefit or harm more than one person, and no one goes
wholly backwards or cross-table. Eventually this situation will end
up with the strongest decks on top as the whole table collapses and
cascades down to the final player. This is, in a sense, the pure form
of cooperation. Your prey is cooperating with you by not walling up.
Your grand-predator is cooperating with you by applying pressure to
your predator. And so on. This, I think, is the scenario in which
you are looking for balance (and for the most part it is there), and
then you are complaining that this scenario doesn't happen, so you
think the game is unbalanced.

But there are other forms of cooperation. There are cross-table
deals, agreements by the whole table to shut down one deck, votes,
rush, Boons, bounce, Folderol (or Ignis Fatuus) and so on. There are
a wide variety of possibilities for engendering cooperation between
players all over the table. The player who maximizes this cooperation
for their own benefit will win almost every time. Ultimately it is
the combination of card variety and this multiplayer cooperation that
balances the game. It doesn't matter that X card or X vampire or X
clan is "out of balance". What matters is that there is a massive
(and growing) variety of options for playing the game on an individual
level, and this leads to an increasingly complex multiplayer
environment. This complexity is how the "self-balance" mentioned by
other people comes about. And this is why I like the genetics
comparison so much - increasing the complexity and variety of the game
leads to an increased number of viable species (decks).

-Volya42

It looks like you're trying to make two or three different points here
(all of which I agree with):
1) If White Wolf attempts to hammer the CCG peg into the RPG hole,
they'll end up with Gothemon, or Gothe-Poke-Digi-Yu-Gi-mon, or
similarly-styled marketing spoo.
2) The same attribute set (Disciplines, clan, special abilities,
title, and age) has CCG impact that varies from the RPG.
3) Point (1) can be achieved by driving the CCG design directly from
an independent RPG design.

I'll fill in the 4th point, which you seem to skip or assume:
4) Since the scope of new V:TES cards is limited to the RPG canon,
the CCG is designed directly from the RPG, and is thrown out of
kilter.

Point (4) is not necessarily true, because limited scope does not
always imply derived design.

And since I haven't gone on a good wandering ramble in a while, here
are some musings on balance...

[ramble]
It would help if you post your definition of 'balance.' For lack of a
common definition, I'll define 'balance' as the marginal probability,
given a table of players who posess identical skills in construction
and play, that one player/deck combination has a better chance of
winning, over the others.

Consider a CCG as a game whose cards modify the base rules. Each
player has a fixed number of cards, a deck(s), with which to change
the rules. Card order within a deck is random, so each instance of a
game will (effectively) deviate from the base rules in its own,
practically unique fashion.

V:TES has the added twist of a 'controller' deck (crypt) which puts
limits (via skills, clans, titles, etc.) on the scope of playable
variance. Hence, the cards, and their rules changes, can be lumped
into deck types [insert reams of past deck type discussion here],
usually supported by several clan/skill combinations, which focus the
rules deviance in different ways.

A deck could be composed of one or more types (Bruise and Bleed, for
example), implemented with differing clan/skill combos (pot/dom vs.
ani/vic). Varying shuffles and game events would alter the prominence
of those types in a game, so the balance question splits into two:
balance of a single game, and balance of a series of games.
Single-game balance is based more on the specific seating arrangements
and shuffles at hand for the particular game, while series-balance is
based more on a track record over several (if not many) games, and the
tendencies of deck types and their implementations.

For basing cards from an RPG, an RPG feature (vampire, story event,
ability, etc.) provides, at least, the color, flavor, and/or
requirements for a card. The feature's effect could and should be
loosely translated into CCG terms, possibly picked from one of several
of the feature's effects.

For a game like V:TES, which should still peg its success on gameplay
instead of cross-marketing potential, it's incumbent on the CCG
designer(s) to ensure that the translation is handled in such a way as
to preserve gameplay. For V:TES, I think the translation has been
handled very well.
[/ramble]

on the level of play in friendly games before you start the game
(powergaming or not).

accept the fact that every one else is going to powergame, so you
might as well do the same, or try to invent your own deck-idea with a
huge risk of being trashed and run over !!

I don't think it's that hard to achieve a well-balanced game, and VTES
would really suck IMO if all cards&clans where more or less equally

I don't think 'reading the table' just involves the future - though
certainly, that's a good part of it.

Can you guess what other people can drag out of their arses to foil you
completely? Assume I decide I want to hop in with my Dramatic Upheaval,
and get your prey. Based on what's gone before, will the rest of the
table be able to pull enough intercept out to stop me? How about votes?
Well, I've seen him play a few votes but he's been discarding them and
it's a mixed deck...

Then there's the question of how players will react - not just in terms
of what they'll play, but how it will influence their future actions.
That's not quite predicting the future game state, if I can draw the
distinction.

Childmonkey puts in Govern the Unaligned, Conditioning, Shadow Play and
Pentex Loves you in his deck, expecting to use them all for the same
bleed. And proceeds to do that at the first possible opportunity. How
is childmonkey's prey going to react? Will he view childmonkey as the
uber-threat and rush backwards to kill childmonkey? Will he wall up so
that the childmonkey can be got rid off and he'll survive? Will the
rest of the table go "Oh, shit!" and gang up on the childmonkey? Is
that reading players, or the table? Well, I'd tend to conflate the two
into one, for purposes of "reading the table".

A lot of that sort of thing is going to get down to how well you can
read a poker face, though.

I can't beleive I have to explain this, especially with a background
in literature, but the basic economic theories of capitalism dictate
that jobs like this are necessary in order to perpetuate the economy.
There has to be museum guards and burger flippers and trash
collectors, so that there can be software developers and investment
bankers. Indeed, this is one of the classic criticisms of capitalism,
this imbalance of job income that creates a class system, and the fact
that built into this system is a self-perpetuation of the class
system, ie: with noted exceptions, the argument is, "the rich get
richer while the poor stay poor." Not that I necessarily agree with
this, but such is the basic theory. So the question is not whether or
not the jobs are useless, they by definition cannot be useless because
they perform a necessary function in their respective economic niche.
That makes the real question one of the employee, not the employment.

SO, given this, you must mean useless in a more philosophical sense. I
can bite that line of reasoning too: useless to whom? If you or your
friend are dissatisfied with your career choices, is that the fault of
the career? What if I personally found the job of museum security
guard truly fulfilling? (and with a fecking lit degree, that's
probably where I'll end up anyhow!) What if my personality was
distinctly suited to fixing things that might otherwise be more
cheaply replaced? Still useless? Only to you and your friend. And this
argument is stunningly applicable to V:TES: Card utility is defined by
environment. What makes a card useful is literally the deck and game
in which it appears. Freak drive is useless in a mono-obfuscate deck,
fer crissake.

Ok, then, let's take this line of reasoning further and apply it to
your reason for starting this thread... your personal dissatisfaction
with V:TES of late, and the possibility that this may relate somehow
to game balance. If you are bored with V:TES, perhaps, like your
career dissatisfaction, this is a personal problem, not something
intrinsic to the game design or balance...

There is a saying here that was very effective up until the point some
pop band co-opted it for their cheese-ass song lyrics, but I think
despite it's cultural dillution it remains true: "you're only bored if
you're boring." The nice thing about V:TES is that given the 500+
crypt cards and 1000+ library cards, YOU have the tools to change this
boredom. You need not be bored, you need not feel the game is flawed
or imbalanced, and you sure as hell don't have to wait for the game
designers to create a new set every 9 months or for LSJ to "fix"
things that are allegedly broken. If, as you note, the problem is such
that you cannot win games even when playing with amateur or unskilled
opponents, then the problem is probably the decks you are playing. To
win, to really sweep tables and maximize victory points, you need a
deck that controls the table, not just a stack of cards that focus on
ousting prey and foiling predator. The above suggestion to include
Dramatic Upheavals is an excellent one. Or, maybe a review of the
tournament winning deck archive is in order.

Basically, OWN YOUR FEELINGS, big guy. You don't have to be bored,
dissatisfied, or disgusted with V:TES, it's *YOUR* choice. Not a
single game designer, nor any posters on this newsgroup are
responsible for your unhappiness. Only you get to chose that.

That's my $11.98 cents worth.

On 5 May 2003 10:23:24 -0700, vermillian wrote:

>I would like to hear this forum's thoughts on this issue. With in your
>post, please remark if you find VTES to be balanced or not, and give
>some reasons why you think it has balance, and I would also like you
>to comment on a statement I've typed below.

In an absolute sense the game is clearly not balanced because it
contains at least one card - Return to Innocence - which is banned
from tournament play for that reason. Most other comparable CCGs are
not flawed in this way.

Folk here will tend to dismiss that because they only play the game
using tournament rules. But that's not really a fair test because
tournament rules are not the game as designed and sold.

One fundamental flaw in VTES' balance is that it is generally agreed
to be unsatisfactory when played with just two players. Shadowfist is
similar but better in this respect because it also has 2-player
tournaments and players who prefer playing the game in that mode.
Other multi-player CCGs like L5R and LotR tend to be better in
2-player form. The only CCG in my experience which is satisfactory
with any number of players is Doomtown - I have as much fun playing it
with 10 players as with 2.

Of course, these are all fairly good CCGs. There are plenty of CCGs
which are quite lacking in balance. A good recent example is the
Buffy CCG. This had huge potential but its early execution was
bungled and now its demise has been announced. With lots of errata
and revision, one might make something of it - I recently opened some
pre-constructed starters for The Wish and was quite impressed at how
improved the game looked. But it's not going to happen - I just don't
think it has enough of a fanbase to keep going.

But games don't need to be balanced to survive - Magic seems to manage
it with a dynamic equilibrium. Other games survive on the strength of
their marketing or licence, e.g. Dragonball-Z. TANJ...

Andrew

something i personally have put a lot of time into, for the simple
reason that it used to be the case that i built all the decks for our
little family/friends play-group, and so's to keep my friends and not
be compelled to sleep in the bath i used to do this in such a way that
all the decks were sorta balanced vis-a-vis one another.

i think your point about how the game is sold is a particularly good
one, because i think it emphasises the fact that we've rather lost
touch with the original idea of CCGs, namely that people would play
with LIMITED pools of cards. Garfield simply didn't realise that the
punters would be STUPID enough to fork out THOUSANDS of negotiable
bills for little bits of pasteboard. Now he is wiser, and richer; and

original error.

Personally i still prefer the form of the game in which one builds
decks from limited pools of cards. In that format i would argue that
RtI is not a problem. But i like both forms, really.

On 13 May 2003 07:21:08 -0700, legbiter wrote:

>Well, i'm not sure if i agree with that. For example, amn't i right in
>thinking there is a problem with It Was A Mountain Lion in Doomtown?

There was but the card got errata. And the game got a rule change
which limited events generally after I won the world championship with
a deck which used lots of them. But I can still play Mountain Lions
in tournaments. You can't play Return to Innocence in VTES
tournaments even though it has official errata. I see this as an
admission of failure though it's only one card, of course.

>And isn't VTES the only CCG with NO card limits? Isn't it, in this
>sense, not comparable to ANY other CCG?

It has different card limits. There's a deck minimum and maximum
unlike, Shadowfist say, in which your deck can be as large or small as
you like. There's a uniqueness rule. And there are quite tough
limits on repeat play of cards which serve much the same function as
the card-multiple limit in other games. The game was clearly broken
when it didn't have these, e.g. vote pushing.

>Personally i still prefer the form of the game in which one builds
>decks from limited pools of cards. In that format i would argue that
>RtI is not a problem. But i like both forms, really.

It's interesting that the HeroClix World Championships are going to be
sealed box events. I suppose that's because they haven't yet got to
grips with imbalances in that game and don't want to risk being
embarrassed by a surfeit of Firelords as at the last two UK
Championships. Part of the trouble is that that game doesn't have the
equivalent of a card limit - you can put as many Firelords or Con
Artists on your team as you can afford. Many venues have a "no-dupes"
rule which is like a card limit of 1 and you often get protracted
debates about this which resemble the CL threads here. Plus ça
change...

Andrew
